articles.title: Checking a freestanding coat stand for stability
articles.summary: A freestanding coat stand can become unsteady when hooks are unevenly loaded or the base is damaged.

visual.alt: A three-point observation checklist identifies the base of a freestanding coat stand, its hooks, and the nearby walking route. It does not show a load test or repair.
visual.caption: Inspect the stand and its surroundings without applying extra force.

sections.title: Check the stand in its normal position
paragraphs: Look for an uneven base, loose-looking hooks, damaged feet and a lean that was not present when the stand was new. Keep children and pets away from an unstable stand rather than testing it by pulling on the hooks.
Compare the stand with the manufacturer's instructions and any load markings. A stand intended for light outerwear may not be suitable for heavy bags or a cluster of wet coats.

sections.title: Keep the entryway usable
paragraphs: Notice whether hanging items protrude into a doorway or narrow walking route. Move ordinary belongings out of the path without handling a stand that appears ready to fall.
Avoid using hooks as climbing aids or supporting a person with the stand. If it wobbles in everyday use, stop loading it until the cause is assessed.

sections.title: Choose a sensible follow-up
paragraphs: Photograph visible wear and record the product name, where available, before seeking replacement parts or support.
If a joint, base or hook is cracked or the stand cannot remain upright, retire it from use rather than improvising a load-bearing repair.

articles.title: Recognising wear in a removable ironing-board cover
articles.summary: An ironing-board cover should fit its particular board and remain in suitable condition for the appliance and fabric being used.

visual.alt: A checklist marks the ironing-board cover surface, the fabric edges and the overall fit, all inspected while the iron is off and cool.
visual.caption: Check a cool board and use compatible manufacturer-approved covers.

sections.title: Identify the cover and padding
paragraphs: Check the board manufacturer's guidance for compatible covers, heat resistance and any separate padding. A decorative fabric alone is not proof of suitability for ironing.
Look for scorching, thinning, torn seams or an exposed metal board surface when the board is cool and not in use. Do not assess damage by reheating a questionable cover.

sections.title: Observe fit without heat
paragraphs: With the iron disconnected and cool, look for bunching, slipping or loose drawcords on the cover. Keep long cords away from children and walking routes.
A cover that shifts unexpectedly may make ordinary ironing less predictable. Stop using a damaged or poorly fitted cover until an appropriate replacement is available.

sections.title: Record and replace appropriately
paragraphs: Keep the board's model or dimensions with the cover packaging or product instructions so a replacement can be matched without guesswork.
Follow the cover and iron manufacturers' directions; never cover vents or alter the board's structural fittings to make an incompatible cover fit.

articles.title: Checking laundry-basket handles and rim damage
articles.summary: Cracked basket handles and sharp rim edges can make ordinary laundry carrying uncomfortable or unreliable.

visual.alt: The visual identifies the laundry basket grip, the top rim and the intended load as separate considerations, without showing a lifting technique.
visual.caption: An intact grip and smooth rim matter as much as basket capacity.

sections.title: Identify the carrying points
paragraphs: Check whether the basket has moulded handles, separate grips or an open rim. The intended carrying method may differ between flexible baskets and rigid containers.
With the basket empty, look for cracks, rough plastic edges or loosened grips. Avoid flexing a damaged handle to see whether it will hold.

sections.title: Review everyday use
paragraphs: Notice whether a loaded basket obstructs the person's view or requires an awkward grip on stairs. A smaller load or different container may be more practical.
Do not lift a heavy basket by one damaged handle. Keep damaged containers out of routes where children might catch clothing or skin on a sharp edge.

sections.title: Choose a replacement
paragraphs: Record the approximate basket size and preferred grip style before replacing a worn item.
Do not rely on tape or glue as a structural handle repair for a basket that will carry substantial weight.

articles.title: Inspecting a removable soap dish and its drainage tray
articles.summary: A removable soap dish can trap moisture or become unstable when its tray is poorly seated.

visual.alt: A three-part schematic checklist names the soap dish, its removable drainage insert and the countertop surface beneath it.
visual.caption: Check moisture and stability before returning the dish to use.

sections.title: Identify the separate pieces
paragraphs: Determine whether the soap dish is a loose countertop item, a removable insert or a wall-mounted accessory. Do not attempt to detach fixed fittings.
Check the maker's cleaning guidance and the surface beneath the dish; some finishes are vulnerable to standing moisture.

sections.title: Check accessible condition
paragraphs: With the dish empty, look for cracks, sharp edges, residue and pooled water. Check whether any removable drainage insert sits flat.
A dish near a basin edge can be knocked onto the floor. Keep it away from the edge and avoid placing it where it interferes with tap controls.

sections.title: Maintain a practical routine
paragraphs: Clean and dry removable pieces according to their material and manufacturer instructions, then confirm that the dish sits securely.
If the dish is broken or the mounting is loose, stop using the affected accessory rather than attaching an improvised heavy replacement.

articles.title: Recognising worn adjustable feet on lightweight furniture
articles.summary: Adjustable feet may be fitted to lightweight tables and storage stands, but they are not a substitute for safe load-bearing design.

visual.alt: A schematic checklist names the visible levelling foot, the floor contact area and the furniture's observed stability, without depicting adjustment or lifting.
visual.caption: Use manufacturer-specific parts and avoid manipulating heavy furniture.

sections.title: Identify the fitted foot
paragraphs: From a normal viewing position, note whether the furniture has a threaded levelling foot, a fixed glide or a manufacturer-specific base.
Look for missing caps, a visibly bent stem or floor marks without tilting, lifting or crawling beneath a heavy item.

sections.title: Observe stability in normal use
paragraphs: Notice whether the furniture rocks during ordinary use or has begun marking the floor. Do not perform a push or tipping test on loaded furniture.
Keep heavy cabinets, shelving and appliances out of this routine; instability or anchoring concerns on those items require suitable professional or manufacturer guidance.

sections.title: Plan the right action
paragraphs: Record the make, model and the affected corner for a manufacturer or competent repairer.
Do not substitute random screws or supports for a missing levelling foot. If the furniture is unstable, stop using it until properly assessed.

articles.title: Checking accessible wheels on a vacuum cleaner floor head
articles.summary: Small wheels and rollers on a vacuum floor head may collect fibres or show wear that affects movement.

visual.alt: A nonprocedural checklist labels the vacuum floor head, its externally visible wheels and the floor surface where marks may appear.
visual.caption: External inspection only; powered components are not opened.

sections.title: Identify the floor head
paragraphs: Read the vacuum model's instructions to distinguish a passive floor head from a powered brush head. Some heads contain electrical connections or moving parts.
Disconnect the appliance from power and allow moving parts to stop before looking at any removable accessory. Do not open a powered head or expose internal wiring.

sections.title: Look at accessible surfaces
paragraphs: From the outside, note trapped hair, visibly cracked wheels, damaged edges or marks left on flooring. Do not pry at a wheel that the instructions do not identify as user-removable.
Check the floor-head type against the floor covering's care instructions; the wrong accessory can mark delicate surfaces.

sections.title: Record and escalate
paragraphs: Keep the exact floor-head model and observed symptoms with the appliance manual. Use only approved user-maintenance steps from the manufacturer.
If a powered head smells hot, makes abnormal noise or has damaged insulation, stop using it and seek appropriate servicing rather than continuing to test it.

articles.title: Checking removable furniture corner guards
articles.summary: Removable corner guards can become detached or damaged, and should not be treated as a substitute for supervision or safe furniture placement.

visual.alt: The checklist identifies a corner guard, its attachment edge and the furniture corner beneath, with no fitting instructions.
visual.caption: A corner guard is supplementary protection, not a structural repair.

sections.title: Identify the guard type
paragraphs: Check whether the guard is a removable adhesive accessory or an integrated part of the furniture. Read the product's age, placement and material warnings.
Look for peeling edges, cracked material or a loose guard without pulling at it in front of young children.

sections.title: Consider the surrounding space
paragraphs: A detached small guard may become a choking hazard. Keep loose pieces away from children and follow the product's safety instructions.
Check whether the furniture edge itself is damaged or sharp. A soft accessory cannot correct a broken structural corner.

sections.title: Plan follow-up
paragraphs: Record the guard brand and furniture surface before seeking a suitable replacement.
If a guard repeatedly detaches or leaves a hazard, remove the affected item from children's access and seek an appropriate alternative rather than layering unknown adhesives.

articles.title: Checking the fit of a removable household mop head
articles.summary: A removable mop head needs to match its handle and attachment system to stay secure during ordinary floor cleaning.

visual.alt: The diagram labels the mop handle, its compatible connector and the removable cleaning head, indicating parts to identify rather than a repair sequence.
visual.caption: Match removable heads to the exact connection type.

sections.title: Identify the connection
paragraphs: Check whether the mop uses a clip, hook-and-loop pad, threaded head or proprietary fitting. Match the exact model before buying replacement parts.
Inspect the detached washable head only as the manufacturer permits, and check for worn fabric, damaged seams or a cracked plastic backing.

sections.title: Observe fit and storage
paragraphs: If the head detaches unexpectedly during normal use, stop and review compatibility rather than forcing it into place.
Keep a damp mop head away from sensitive flooring and storage surfaces. Follow the product's washing and drying instructions to prevent avoidable residue or odour.

sections.title: Keep a maintenance note
paragraphs: Record the mop model, compatible head type and replacement date if useful for shared household supplies.
Discard a head with sharp damaged parts or a connection that will not hold securely; avoid improvised fasteners that could scratch floors.
